- Multi-agent Systems Explained in 17 Minutes: Kind: captions Language: en Hey everyone, I'm Shaw. In this video, I'm going to explain multi-agent systems. I'll start with an overview of what they are and when to use them and then review four ways we can build multi- aent systems with concrete examples. 2025 was the year of AI agents. This is where we saw the rise of deep research agents and coding agents which are driving a significant portion of AI's economic value. And the key principle that made this possible is this idea of more tokens lead to better performance. In other words, as agents think for longer and longer, execute more tool calls, and interact more with the real world, the better they are able to accomplish tasks. The technical term for this principle is so-called testime compute scaling. This shifted the AI space from only focusing on training bigger and bigger models to focusing on how we can get these models to generate more and more tokens. Although test time compute scaling is a powerful and flexible way we can get more value out of AI, there is a problem which is that single AI agents have a finite context window. And even if we have these very large context windows like a million tokens and beyond, there is this phenomenon of context rot where as the context window gets filled up with more and more tokens, performance actually tends to drop in these models. This was shown by research from Chroma DB where they had the various frontier models do a very simple task of word repetition and as the context window got more and more full there was a clear drop in the models performance. This brings up a tension between this idea of more tokens leads to better performance and if the context window gets too full performance drops. And so how can we get the best of both worlds where we can get these models to generate the maximum number of tokens without seeing this drop in performance? One way we can do this is through multi- aent systems. So instead of just relying on a single AI agent, we can get multiple AI agents to work together. There are a lot of different ways this can look as we'll talk about in a little bit. But the reason that this can be advantageous is that it can scale up test time compute while mitigating the risks of context rot. Another key benefit is that if you have multiple agents working together, they can work in parallel. So, for example, if you have a research agent, instead of just having one trying to research sources one at a time, you can spin up dozens of research agents to independently look up different keywords or investigate different sources in parallel and then come back together to synthesize their findings. And then finally, with multi- aent systems, you can have specialized agents. So, just like how teams of humans working together can benefit from specialization, the same thing's true for AI agents. So you can create these curated sets of instructions and tools for each agent for performing a particular task. While there are these advantages of multi- aent systems over single agent systems, it's not a cure all. In other words, there are clear instances where single agent systems are better than multi- aent ones. And one of the core differentiators is that if you're performing sequential tasks where an agent needs to execute an action, get information, and perhaps update its plan or perhaps use that new information to execute the next task, using a single agent system is going to be more effective than a multi- aent one. On the other hand, if the task is decomposible, meaning that it can be split into parallel subtasks or the context can be split into smaller chunks that are independent, then multi- aent systems can be helpful. For example, if we have a sequential task like look up the latest documentation for Chroma DB, use that to create a PRD or a plan for the application that you're trying to build, and then finally build the application. You can't come up with a plan before looking at the documentation and you can't code up the project before coming up with a plan. So each of these tasks has to be performed in this particular order. On the other side, decomposible tasks like research is a great example here where agents can explore different research directions. So if instead of looking up specifically Chroma DB's documentation, maybe you want to research all the different rag solutions that are currently available today. You can have multiple agents going out in parallel, one looking up chroma, one looking up cohhere, one looking up llama index and so on and so forth. So you can have multiple agents going out doing a deep dive into each of these libraries and then those results can be synthesized later. Another key insight comes from this paper by Google research where they found if a single agent system can do the task more than 45% of the time, using a multi- aent system is not a good idea. And this is basically because as you scale your system to using multiple agents instead of one. This creates a coordination task. So basically there's going to be computational costs for having these agents effectively collaborate with one another. Above this 45% mark, there's not a significant increase in performance that justifies the coordination costs associated with multi- aent systems. If your single agent system is successful more than 45% of the time, just stick with that. If it fails more than 45% of the time, multi- aent systems might be able to help. And finally, if cost is the most important factor in your system, so you want to keep compute costs down, then a single agent system is going to be the way to go. However, if cost isn't the most important factor, and really what you're trying to do is maximize performance because the economic value is there for the particular use case you're working on, then a multi- aent system can make sense. Ultimately, AI agents burn a lot of compute. And so if you go from one AI agent to let's say 5 10 15 20 of them working together, this is going to not only linearly increase the compute cost, but there's going to be a super linear increase in compute costs because there's going to be some additional compute required to get all of them to talk to each other. So in other words, a multi- aent system with five agents will have more than 5x the compute costs of a single agent system. Typically, it's going to be a good idea to start with your single agent system. Mainly so you can evaluate how well it can do this particular task. Then only once all these different criteria are satisfied would it make sense to transition to a multi- aent system. Okay, so we've talked about what multi- aent systems are and when to use them. Now I want to walk through four specific architectures for building these systems. These are based on this paper by Google which is reference number four. There they define these four key categories of independent multi- aent systems, decentralized ones, centralized ones, and hybrid. So I'm going to talk through each of these one at a time. Starting with architecture one, independent multi-agent systems. This is just running isolated agents in parallel. Imagine you send a request to an agent, but instead of just doing this once, you do this any number of times. Maybe you do this like five or 10 times, but you're just sending the same request to every single agent and none of the agents are talking to each other. So, they're each just trying to execute this task on their own. And then at the end, you can aggregate the outputs of these agents through some kind of voting mechanism or you can maybe pick the best option among all the results. An example where this might be helpful is if you're trying to generate a user interface for a application you're building and you just have like a fuzzy idea of what you want to build, but you're not sure on the specifics of what you want. What you could do is give the specifications to three instances of cloud code. For example, these three instances will come up with three different options and then maybe you just pick the best option of the three. The pros of this is that this is very simple to implement and there's no coordination task. But the cons is that because these agents aren't really interacting with one another, you're just running multiple versions of whatever AI agent you have multiple times, usually the gains are just going to be marginal from just using a single agent. And then another downside is that since the agents can't talk to each other, there's no opportunity for error correction. That same paper by Google research found that these independent multi- aent systems will actually have a 17x increase in the number of errors compared to just single agent systems. So this architecture may not make sense for most use cases. The second architecture involves actually allowing these agents to talk to one another in this peer-to-peer network. For example, you can have multiple agents and every agent can talk to every other agent and there's no sort of hierarchy. everyone's on this equal playing field and they're just trying to get the task done with some harness built around them. For example, there was this case study from someone at Anthropic where they had a team of AI agents build this C compiler. So, you can check out the blog post on their website. It's called building a C compiler with a team of parallel clouds. I think it's reference number five. And basically the key points here is that they had 16 agents running over 2 weeks trying to get this task done. The result was about a 100,000line C compiler written in Rust. The API costs were $20,000. So a significant investment and the end result was pretty impressive. So it passed with 99% accuracy on this C compiler benchmark. And it was indeed able to run Doom, which is apparently a benchmark in of itself. And so the key point here is that a C compiler is a massive undertaking that a single agent won't be able to do in of itself. So single agents are great at like building a specific feature in an existing codebase, but building this monolithic large-scale project with a single agent is not feasible. And while this was an expensive project, so it was $20,000 in API costs and it took 2 weeks to create, if one was to hire human developers to build this, maybe it would have taken months instead of weeks and instead of costing on the order of $10,000, it probably would have cost on the order of $100,000. But of course, what expert human developers could come up with would probably be higher quality than what this multi- aent system was able to create. So there's this natural trade-off of like the quality of the final result. So you can sacrifice quality if you want to get it fast and cheap or you can get the highest quality by allowing it to take longer to run with humans and you can pay the humans more than API usage costs. The pros here is that a decentralized multi- aent system is a very simple design. You just have a bunch of agents that can be just exact replicas of one another and then you build some harness around them. This can be like a set of tests to ensure tasks are actually done. It could be a task list where agents can check off and grab tasks off the list and so on and so forth. And this decentralized architecture seems to be good for exploreheavy tasks. They have a couple of benchmarks that they use in reference number four, but decentralized was a top performer for tasks that required a wide breadth of exploration. But the cons of course is that because every agent can talk to every other agent and there's no one clearly in charge, this is going to create the maximum coordination tasks. So in order for the discovery of one agent to make it to the other agents, that agent has to talk to every other agent. So like to send them a message or there could be a shared context that these agents work on but then building this harness is going to become non-trivial and task specific. So on the flip side of decentralized we have a centralized architecture. So instead of just allowing this swarm of agents to attack a problem, you can have agents coordinated by an orchestrator. This will just have some kind of lead agent that will delegate work to a set of workers. For example, this is what Anthropic did when they built this multi- aent research system. So they had a lead agent that had access to a set of tools and that would delegate tasks to specialized sub aents. So there was a citations sub agent and then there were various search agents that could go off and investigate a specific topic and then there was this running memory that the lead agent could put information into. The key pros of the centralized architecture, this turns out to be very effective for error correction. So again referencing that paper from Google, they found that this centralized architecture actually had the lowest error amplification of all these multi-agent architectures. And the reason is if one of the sub agents made a mistake, instead of that mistake being immediately propagated out to all the other agents, it would only make it back to the lead agent which could double check the work and verify that it's correct. The cons of course is that this architecture is pretty complex and then again designing the harness is going to be nontrivial. Finally, we have architecture 4 which kind of gets the best of both worlds of centralized and decentralized. Instead of just having the lead agent be the only one talking to the various sub agents in the centralized architecture, a hybrid approach allows some or all these sub aents to talk to one another. This is exactly how the new feature in cloud code works. Cloud code just released so-called agent teams and this is exactly the architecture they use. They have this main agent that will spin up all the various sub aents and assign tasks to each of the sub aents. There'll be this shared task list and then teammates can pick up work and communicate with one another with the lead agent supervising the whole thing. The pros of this is that you get the benefits of error correction while maintaining the flexibility of the decentralized because the sub agents or these teammates can still talk to one another. So they don't necessarily have to play telephone of passing something to the lead agent who would then pass it to a different sub agent. The cons of course is that this is going to be the most complicated architecture and you're still going to have this coordination tax because the teammates can communicate with one another which is going to increase compute costs and add to the number of tokens each teammate has in their context window. So while multi- aent systems hold a lot of promise for the future of AI, there are still some current limitations. The first and most significant is that there's still not a single optimal architecture. Really what this will boil down to is that the best architecture is going to be use case and task dependent. So for example, maybe swarms are great for unstructured exploratory research tasks while having a centralized approach is going to be great for coherent single goaloriented tasks. This is ultimately just going to depend on the problem you're trying to solve. Another key limitation is that creating an effective harness is going to be non-trivial. And so a harness is just the code and the software that you build around the agents. So this could be things like tests, shared context, task lists, and anything else. Again, this is going to be use case specific. And there's still no clear best practices and standards for doing this effectively, which is just going to require a lot of trial and error for people trying to build multi- aent systems today. Finally, the current heruristics that people are discovering like from the Google paper that I've referenced a few times may become obsolete as the models become smarter. So right now what we're seeing is the results for the current generation of models, but perhaps with the next generation we're going to see new rules because current limitations will just become obsolete. So where does that leave us? What is the future of multi-agent systems? The way I see it, 2025 was the year single agent systems became good. In my opinion, 2026 is going to be the year that multi-agent systems become good. Because at this point, the models are indeed good enough to create these multi-agent systems. It's just now an engineering problem. It's mainly the challenge of building an effective harness for the specific task. Another key point here is that multi-agent systems are not a so-called paro improvement of single agent systems. So, in other words, multi-agent systems do not dominate single agent ones across all tasks. It's only when tasks are decomposable that multi- aent systems are going to be valuable. So again, sequential tasks use a single agent system. Decomposible tasks use a multi- aent system. Finally, the harness is the hard part today and defining the optimal architecture is going to depend on the task. So at the two extremes, we have the decentralized architecture which is like a swarm of agents attacking a problem. On the other side, we have the centralized architecture where there's a lead agent delegating tasks and then there's a hybrid which is something in the middle. It's going to be worth experimenting with different architectures to see which one is going to work best for your specific use case. So, if you have any questions about any of the topics I discussed here or have any suggestions for future content, please let me know in the comments below. And as always, thank you so much for your time and thanks for watching.

  10. @iosascha1: The 4-architecture taxonomy (independent → hybrid) is a clean framework. In practice, what I've seen push teams from centralized to hybrid is cost predictability. With a pure centralized orchestrator, the supervisor agent becomes both a bottleneck and a cost multiplier - it needs to understand every subtask well enough to route it, which often means using an expensive model for the orchestrator itself. The hybrid approach lets you cascade: cheap classifier model decides the architecture per-task ("this is simple, run independent" vs "this needs coordination, use centralized"), then the chosen architecture runs with model tiers matched to step complexity. Net result: 40-50% lower inference cost than always-centralized, with only ~3% quality degradation on benchmarks. One limitation I'd add to the MAS list: debugging multi-agent failures is exponentially harder. Structured decision logging at every agent boundary is non-negotiable in production.

Have you ever wondered why certain artificial intelligence systems act like they are part of a community? The answer lies in the fascinating world of multi- aent systems. These systems consist of multiple autonomous agents that interact within a shared environment. Each agent makes decisions based on its own perceptions, goals, and interactions with other agents. Social behaviors in these systems emerge from how agents communicate, cooperate, compete, or coordinate with each other. They often follow predefined rules or learn from their experiences using techniques like reinforcement learning. This means that while each agent operates independently, they can exchange information and adapt their behavior based on what others are doing. Think about traffic simulations. Individual vehicle agents follow simple rules like maintaining safe distances and changing lanes. However, when you look at the bigger picture, these simple rules lead to realistic traffic patterns such as traffic jams or smooth flows, all without a central control system. The design of multi- aent systems aims to model interactions that reflected real world social dynamics. From the perspective of machine learning, especially reinforcement learning, agents learn to maximize their own rewards while considering the actions of other agents. This naturally leads to social behaviors as they negotiate shared resources or goals. - Context Engineering vs. Prompt Engineering: Smarter AI with RAG & Agents: Kind: captions Language: en I think by now most of us are familiar with the term prompt engineering. It's the process of crafting the input text used to prompt a large language model, including instructions and examples and formatting cues. It's what steers the LLM's behavior and output. Now, context engineering, on the other hand, is the broader discipline of programmatically assembling everything the LLM sees during inference. Now that includes prompts, but also retrieve documents and memory and tools—everything needed to deliver accurate responses. So, to demonstrate the difference, let me introduce you to an agentic AI model that I like to call Graeme. Secret Agent Graeme. Agent Graeme specializes in travel booking. So, if I send Graeme this prompt, "Book me a hotel in Paris for the DevOps conference next month," well, the agent responds with "Sure thing. The Best Western Paris Inn has great wifi and free parking. It's booked." Cool. But the only trouble is the Best Western is located in Paris, Kentucky, and that DevOps conference is in Paris, France. Now, you could argue that that's a failing of prompt engineering. I wasn't specific on the location. But it could also be seen as a failing of context engineering because if Agent Graeme here was just a little smarter, well, they could have used a tool to check my calendar or look up the conference online to find the right location. So ... so let's try again with a follow-up prompt. My conference is in Paris, France. €900 a night. Ritz booked. Champagne. Breakfast included. Well, uh, wish me luck getting that one approved through my company expense reimbursement system. But Graeme here can't really be blamed for that one because I didn't provide sufficient context. I should have made my company's travel policy available to the agent. Perhaps there's a JSON file specifying things like maximum permissible hotel rates for the area. So, prompt engineering—that's the craft of wording the instruction itself. And context engineering is the system-level discipline of providing the model with what it needs to plausibly accomplish the task. So let's take a look at these two terms a bit closer. And we'll start with the key techniques that make prompt engineering effective. Now this is part art, part science. But there are several prompt engineering techniques that are now widely adopted. So, take for example, role assignment. This tells the LLM who it should be. So, you are a senior Python developer reviewing code for security vulnerabilities. Well, that produces vastly different outputs than a more generic code review request. The model adopts the expertise, the vocabulary and the concerns of that persona that we asked for. Uh ... another good technique comes down to few shot examples. So, this is show, don't just tell. So, providing 2 or 3 examples of input/output pairs ... that helps the model understand your exact format and style requirements. So, if you want JSON output with specific field names, well, show it. Show it in the examples. Now, before we had reasoning models trained on reinforcement learning, a pretty popular prompt engineering technique was called COT or chain of thought prompting. Now this forces the model to show its work. Adding "let's think step by step" or "explain your reasoning"—that prevents the LLM from jumping to conclusions. And it's particularly powerful for complex reasoning tasks. And then another technique is called constraint setting. Here you define boundaries explicitly. So, "limit your response to only 100 words" or "only use information from the provided context". And that helps prevent the model from going off on tangents. Context engineering—that helps build dynamic, agentic systems to orchestrate the entire agentic environment. And let's take a look at some of the components of that. Well, agentic AI. First of all, it needs memory. And memory management can be thought of in two forms. So there's short-term memory ... that might involve summarizing long conversations to stay within context windows so that past conversations are not forgotten. And then there's also long-term memory, and that uses vector databases to retrieve things like user preferences and past trips and learned patterns. Then there is state management. Now, this says where are we in a multi-step process? So, if an agent is booking a complete trip—the flight, the hotel, the ground transportation, all of it— well, the agent needs to maintain state across these operations. Did the flight booking succeed? What's the arrival time for scheduling the airport transfer? Stuff like that. So, state ensures that the agent doesn't lose context mid task. Now, another important component is retrieval augmented generation or RAG, that connects an agent to dynamic knowledge sources. So, RAG uses hybrid search which combines semantic and keyword matching based on context. So, when retrieving your company's travel policy, RAG isn't returning the entire travel policy document. There's a lot of stuff that's just kind of irrelevant to the context in there. So instead, it's picking out the relevant sections and the relevant exceptions and returning only those contextually relevant parts back to the agent. And agents also need access to tools so they can actually go out and do stuff. So LLMs by themselves, they can't check real databases or call APIs or execute code. It's tools that bridge that gap, and a tool might query a SQL database, or it might fetch live pricing data, it might deploy infrastructure. And where context engineering comes in is in defining the interfaces that guide the LLM toward the correct usage. And tool descriptions— they specify what the tool does, when to use it, and what constraints apply. And prompt engineering? Well, actually we should include that as well because that is also part of context engineering. You can take a base written prompt like "analyze security logs for anomalies". You can take that as your prompt and then at runtime, inject the prompt with current context, like recent alerts and known false positives. And all of those variables in the prompt, they get populated from the states and the memory and the RAG retrievals. So, that final prompt might be 80% dynamic content from there and 20% static instructions. So, prompt engineering ... it gives you better questions. Context engineering—that gives you better systems when you combine them properly. Hotel booked. Paris, France. Under budget. Near the venue. Excellent. Thank you, Agent Graeme. Pending approval from your manager, HR and finance. Estimated approval time: 6 to 8 weeks. Uh, the conference is in two weeks. Have you tried prompt engineering your manager?

- LangChain vs LangGraph: A Tale of Two Frameworks: Kind: captions Language: en-US LangChain and LangGraph are both open source frameworks designed to help developers build applications with large language models. So what are the differences and why use one over the other? Well, I think a good place to start. Is to define what these two things are, and let's begin with LangChain. Now, we've done a dedicated video on LangChain, and my guess is there's probably a pop up somewhere over my head right now encouraging you to watch that video. But don't click, not yet. Give me a moment to summarize LangChain. Then at the end of this video, if you want any more, you can go back and check that one out. Okay. Now, at its core, LangChain is a way for building LLM powered applications by executing a sequence of functions in a chain. So let's say we're building an application and the first thing it needs to do is it needs to retrieve some data from a website. Once we've done that, we move on to stage two, And stage two is to summarize that data that we retrieved. And then finally, we're going to use this summary to do something, specifically, We're going to have it answer user questions. So the workflow here is retrieve, summarize, and answer Now we can use the LangChain to help us do this. So let's start with the retrieve component. Now, the retrieve component might consist of a LangChain component called a document loader. Now a document loader is used to fetch and load content from various data sources, and if some of those documents are large, we might choose to use a text splitter, which is another LangChain component to split takes up into smaller, semantically meaningful chunks. Okay, that's retrieve. Now To summarize, we would use a chain, and the chain will orchestrate the summarization process. Now, that might include constructing a prompt component to instruct an LLM to perform the summarization. And that might also contain an LLM component to pass that request to the large language model of our choosing. Okay, and then answer. Well, we would build another chain and this chain might include a memory component, so this is another component of LangChain, and that's used to store conversation, history and context, And we'd throw in another prompt component and another LLM component to generate the answer based on the summary and the record context. And the cool thing here is that the LLM that we use for the answer component, may be a completely different large language model to the one we use in the summarize component. LangChain modular architecture let's build complex workflows by combining these high level components. Okay, now let's introduce LangGraph. LangGraph is a specialized library within the LangChain ecosystem, specifically designed for building stateful multi-agent systems that can handle complex nonlinear workflows. So let's consider a task management assistant agent. Now, the workflow here involves processing user input. So let's start there, Process inputs, And then to this workflow we are going to allow to add tasks, we're going to be able to complete tasks, and we are also going to be able to summarize task. So this is the kind of the architecture of what we're trying to build here. Now, LangGraph helps us create this as a graph structure, where each one of these actions is considered as a node. So at tasks, complete tasks, summarize, they're all nodes. And then the transitions between these things, that's known as edges. Now the central mode is the process input node. So that's where the user input comes in, and that's going to use an LLM component to understand the user intent and to route to the appropriate action node. Now there's another component here that's quite central to this called state, the state component. And the state component is used to maintain the task list across all the interaction. So the adds task node adds new tasks to the state, the complete task node marks tasks as finished, and then the summarize node uses an LLM to generate an overview of current tasks. All nodes can access and modify the state allowing for contextual stateful interactions. The graph structure allows the assistant to handle various user requests in any order, always returning back to the process input node after the action is complete. LangGraph Architecture lets us create flexible stateful agents that can maintain context over extended interactions. So let's directly compare, LangChain and LangGraph across a number of dimensions. Let's start with the primary focus. Now the Primary focus of LangGraph Is to create and manage what is known as multi agent systems and workflows. The focus of LangChain is to provide an abstraction layer for chaining LLM operations into large language model applications. That's the difference between the two. Now, as for. Structure, LangChain adopts no surprise here a chain structure. And that acts as a Dag, that is an acronym for directed acyclic graph, Which means that tasks are executed in a specific order always moving forward. So, for example, we start with task number one then we'd have a branch for maybe tasks number two and task three, and then we'd come back to the central task number four. And this process is great where you know the exact sequence of steps that are needed. Now, LangGraph's graph structure, on the other hand, is a little bit different because it allows for loops and revisiting previous states. So we might have state A which can go backwards and forwards with state B and State C, and this is beneficial for interactive systems where the next step might depend on evolving conditions or user input. Now, when it comes to components, LangChain uses a bunch and we've mentioned many of these already, that includes memory, There's the prompt component as well, There's also the LLM component, which is how we actually pass things to the large language model, And there's the agent component as well that forms, chains between all of these things. Now, LangGraph uses a bunch of different components. So we have nodes, we also have edges, And we have states, and these are all part of a graph. And speaking of state. That brings us nicely to state management. I don't think we can say that LangChain has somewhat limited state management capabilities. It can pass information forth through the chain, but it doesn't easily maintain a persistent state across multiple runs. That said, LangChain does have these memory components that can maintain some state across interactions. LangGraph's state management, I'm going to say, is more robust, And that's because state is a core component that all nodes can access and modify, allowing for more complex, context aware behaviors. Let's say use cases. Well, LangChain really excels, particularly at sequential tasks like a process that retrieves data and then processes it and then outputs a result. Again, that said, LangChain is able to handle non sequential tasks to some extent with its own agents feature, but LangGraph's wheelhouse that really is. Scenarios that have a much more complex nature to them. Complex systems requiring ongoing interaction and adaptation. For example, a virtual assistant that needs to maintain context over long conversations and handle varying types of requests. So that LangChain and LangGraph, two powerful frameworks for building applications that make use of large language models. All right. That's all I got. You can go watch that LangChain video now.

- Multi Agent Systems - a complete guide with hands-on using LangGraph | Agent Design Pattern: Kind: captions Language: en In this video, we are going to look into multi- aent systems. First, we'll start with why we need multi-agent systems when we have so sophisticated single agent systems. We'll motivate as to why we need them. Then, we'll move on to types of different multi-agent collaboration. More specifically, we will look into the structure of multi-agent systems and there are quite a few structures there. Particularly we will implement the hierarchical multi-agent system in Python of course and we will be using the langraph framework for implementation. So let's get started. Now before we jump straight into multi- aent system let's understand what are the problems with single agent system. As the agents become more and more commonplace in today's world the complexity increases. You know the there is always commercial systems are always complicated and so the complexity is quite high. So scaling these agentic systems becomes quite a big challenge like in any organization we have you know we have an accountant we have a lawyer and we also uh have someone who's taking care of commercials and someone who's taking care of technicals. Similarly, we need specializations among these agents. And instead of having a generic single agent that takes care of everything, we feel that specialization and decision branching is crucial for these agentic systems to collaborate and work together. And also there's a need for a error checking. Take an example where we have two agents. One agent is doing the actual task. The other one is actually supervising it. So it makes much more sense for the first one to be corrected whenever it does some mistakes because there's a second agent that's actually monitoring it. So when it comes to error checking and selfcorrection, it's makes sense to have multiple agents. And we also need to combine diverse models. For example, if you're doing a large coding task, we can go for the set model which is uh which is good at coding and then we can have some other model like openAI's GPT models in order to do some analysis or to you know gather some requirements. So combining diverse models is possible if we have multiple agents doing different task. So the solution lies in multi- aent systems. So talking of multi-agent system there's a very nice paper about multi-agent collaboration mechanism and which is a survey of multi-agent systems specific to LLMs and this paper talks of you know different multi- aent system collaborations multi-agent collaboration can be classified based on the type of collaboration for example the agents can be cooperative or competitive one agent is competing against the other and so you get the best performance out of the system or there could be cooperation as to a single goal that they need to achieve. And you can also classify multi- aent collaboration based on the structure. For example, you could have a centralized structure or you could have a distributed one or you could have a hierarchical one. And this hierarchical one is the one that we are going to implement today. And you can also have strategies. For example, it can be rule-based. It can be you know model based and it can even be role based. You can have separate roles for separate agents. For example, in a in a coding task, one can be a reviewer which is which acts as a senior developer and the other one can be an architect agent which is going to actually architect the system. So there are different ways in which multi- aent systems can be coordinated or orchestrated just based on the structure itself. We can have a supervisor agent supervisor as a tool and we can have a network structure, we can have hierarchical structure or we can have custom design. So in case of a network structure, we can have you know agents collaborating like this. In in this example, we have four agents and the communication between the four agents is possible in any direction. So as you can see this could easily lead to chaos because we have not defined the role of each of the agents and each one can do whatever it likes and pass on the control to a different agent. So that leads us to the next type of collaboration which is the supervisor structure. Here we have a well-defined supervisor with which all the other agents are reporting to or communicating to. So the supervisor can nicely coordinate the execution of the task between all the sub aents or the different teams and so there's nice control of the execution of the task. But again the drawback here is that if this if this supervisor agent collapses for some reason then the whole system breaks down. So this becomes a single point of failure. So that's something we need to keep in mind if you are building a supervisor based agentic system. Then comes supervisor as a tool or supervisor tool calling. In this case we have the different agents which expose themselves to the supervisor in the form of a tool. So basically supervisor treats them as a tool rather than an agent and this is a small variation to the supervisor structure and it's called the supervisor as tool or supervisor tool calling. The next type is that of hierarchical where we can see that there is a supervisor on top and below that there is another supervisor but this supervisor agent has a team and it's got two agents reporting to it. So uh so this team has a separate role to play. Similarly on the other side we have a separate supervisor and this supervisor has couple of agents reporting to it and these three together form a team and this team in turn reports to the supervisor. So we can imagine this as kind of how an organization is structured. So we have let's say the CEO or CTO and we have say the technical team which is reporting back to it and the technical team is probably led by a tech lead or somebody else and we have a commercial team that takes care of the commercials and the commercial team again reports back to the head of the organization. So this is the exact structure that we are going to implement today. - CrewAI: Build AI Agent Teams That Actually Collaborate: Kind: captions Language: en What if your AI agents had roles, goals, and backstories, and they could actually collaborate, delegate, and make autonomous decisions as a team? This is the most popular multi-agent framework in the entire Python ecosystem right now. Crew AI is a lean, lightning fast Python framework for orchestrating multi-agent AI systems. It was built entirely from scratch, completely independent of lang chain, and it takes a fundamentally different approach to how agents work together. Instead of chaining individual tool calls, Crew AI models agent collaboration the way human teams actually function. Each agent has a defined role, specific goals, a backstory that shapes its decision-m, and access to tools. Agents are grouped into crews that coordinate through defined processes, sequential, hierarchical with a manager agent or fully autonomous. The framework supports any LLM provider, OpenAI, Anthropic, Olama for local models, and it's MIT licensed, so you can use it anywhere. The number that matters, over 100,000 developers have completed Crew AI certification through deep learning.ai, AI, making it one of the most widely adopted agent frameworks in production today. The core concept in crew AI is the crew, a team of agents working together on a shared objective. Each agent in a crew has genuine autonomy. They don't just execute predefined steps. They make real decisions about how to approach tasks, when to delegate to other agents, and how to handle unexpected situations. A crew defines which agents participate, what tasks need to be completed, and what process governs execution. In sequential mode, tasks run in order with each task building on the previous result. In hierarchical mode, a manager agent coordinates planning and dynamically delegates work to specialist agents. In autonomous mode, agents independently determine their own execution strategy. This isn't prompt chaining. It's actual multi-agent collaboration where the agents negotiate their approach based on their defined expertise and the current state of the work. Crews handle autonomous collaboration, but production systems need more control. That's where flows come in. Flows are Crew AAI's eventdriven workflow engine. They provide granular control over execution paths, state management, and conditional routing. You build flows with Python decorators. The at start decorator marks entry points. At listen triggers steps when specific events complete. At router enables conditional branching based on results. You can combine conditions with or, and operators for complex orchestration logic. State is managed through paidantic models giving you type safety and validation at every step. The key insight is that flows and crews are complimentary. A flow can orchestrate multiple crews routing between them based on results while each crew maintains its own internal autonomous collaboration. This separation between orchestration logic and agent autonomy is what makes Crew AI production ready. Crew AI implements a sophisticated memory system that most agent frameworks skip entirely. Short-term memory tracks the current task context, what the agent has learned during this specific execution. Long-term memory persists across runs, allowing agents to learn from previous executions and improve over time. Entity memory tracks important information about people, organizations, and concepts encountered during work. All three memory types are configurable with retention policies.
